newsitem.title: USA: State prosecutors meet about America Online. [CORRECTED 08:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: State prosecutors meet about America Online. [CORRECTED 08:35 GMT]

text.p: Prosecutors from 20 states met Thursday in response to the tide of customer complaints against America Online Inc., even as the world's biggest online service suffered another spate of embarrassing outages.

"The meeting was called to determine whether an agreement could be reached that would provide some relief for AOL customers, who feel the company is not living up to its pledge to provide unlimited service for $19.95 a month," said Dan Curry, spokesman for Illinois Attorney General Jim Ryan.
(Corrects to make clear that it is the customers who feel the company is not living up to its pledge.)

In another blow to America Online, the Dulles, Va.-based company said it suffered outages Thursday that prevented its more than 8 million subscribers from accessing their electronic mail for more than three hours.
State attorneys general or their aides attended the meeting, some in person, some via conference call, along with attorneys from America Online, participants said.

"They heard our concerns and we asked for a response," said Minnesota Assistant Attorney General Carolyn Ham, who participated in the meeting by telephone. She would not comment on the specifics of what was discussed, or if there was a deadline for a company response.
America Online said it had a constructive meeting with the prosecutors and that it was cooperating with them and addressing their concerns.
America Online stock dropped $2.625 to $37.25 Thursday on the New York Stock Exchange.

America Online has been beset with network problems ever since Dec. 1, when it switched its members over to unlimited usage for a flat rate of $19.95 a month. Previously, most subscribers had paid $9.95 for five hours online a month, with charges for additional time.

An AOL spokeswoman said Thursday that it suffered an e-mail outage from 7:15 a.m. to 9:15 a.m. EST due to a power supply problem and that a circuit board in one of its computers again prevented subscribers from accessing their e-mail, from 12:30 p.m. to 1:40 p.m. EST.

Last week, America Online suffered a partial outage that lasted nearly four hours. Its most publicized outage occurred last August, when the service was down for about 19 hours. America Online said last week it would spend $350 million to upgrade its network, as class-action lawsuits in at least four states were filed against AOL, which has more than 8 million members. The company also appealed to customers to log off the system when not using it.
Customers have flooded the company and state consumer fraud agencies with complaints, saying they are not getting the service that AOL advertised.
"We've seen a great deal of complaints in a short period of time," said Michael Hering, Massachusetts' assistant attorney general for consumer protection, who joined Thursday's meeting by phone.
Hering said "it's a possibility" the attorneys general would file a joint consumer fraud lawsuit.
Typically in such cases, prosecutors from different states band together in a lawsuit, then split the proceeds, or demand a rebate or some other compensation for customers.
The service has said it was not prepared for the positive response to its move to the flat fee.
